blocks.md:
### What makes a model "generative"

A generative model learns the patterns in its training data well enough to produce new examples that fit them. A **large language model (LLM)** is a generative model of text, built on the transformer architecture from Module 1.1 and trained on enormous amounts of text and code. "Large" refers to its parameter count, typically billions, and to the scale of its training data.

At its core an LLM performs **next-token prediction**. Given a sequence of tokens, it outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary, typically tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand entries. One token is selected, appended, and the process repeats. Everything an LLM appears to do, from answering questions to writing code, emerges from this single repeated step and the patterns it learned in training.

That has three practical consequences:

- **There is no lookup of facts.** The model generates what is statistically plausible given its training and context. Plausible and true usually coincide, but not always, which is why hallucination exists.
- **Output length drives cost and latency.** Every generated token requires a full pass through the model.
- **Everything in the context shapes the output.** The system instructions, the user’s words, retrieved documents and tool results all feed the same prediction.

### Decoding: how a token is chosen

The strategy for picking each token is called **decoding** or **sampling**:

- **Greedy decoding** always takes the single most likely token. It is predictable but can be repetitive.
- **Temperature** rescales the probabilities before sampling. Low values (towards 0) concentrate on the most likely tokens; high values (around 1 and above) spread choice across less likely ones.
- **Top-k** sampling limits choice to the k most likely tokens. **Top-p** (nucleus) sampling limits choice to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, for example 0.9.
- **Maximum tokens** caps how much the model may generate, and **stop sequences** end generation when a given string appears.

These are configuration settings, which makes them part of the system you secure. A deployment that lets users set very high token limits invites cost abuse, and one that runs extraction tasks at high temperature invites inconsistent results.

blocks.title: The stages of building an LLM
items: Pretraining

The model learns language, facts and reasoning patterns by predicting the next token across trillions of tokens of text and code. It is **self-supervised** and consumes most of the compute. The result is a **base model**: fluent, knowledgeable, but not reliably helpful or safe. Whatever was in the training data, including errors, bias and harmful content, can surface later.
Instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning)
The base model is trained on curated examples of requests and good responses, teaching it to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
Preference tuning

People compare model responses and rank them. **Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)** trains a reward model on those rankings and optimises the LLM against it. Alternatives such as **direct preference optimisation (DPO)** learn from preference pairs directly. This stage instils much of the helpful, honest and harmless behaviour people expect.
Safety testing and red teaming

Developers evaluate the model against benchmarks and adversarial tests for harmful capabilities, bias and policy violations, then mitigate what they find. Testing reduces risk but can’t prove its absence.
Release
The model is deployed behind an API, embedded in products, or published as **open weights**. Each route moves different security responsibilities to the people who deploy it.

blocks.md:
### Multimodal models

**Multimodal** models handle more than one type of data. **Vision-language models** accept images, screenshots or scanned documents with text and reason about them together. **Speech** models transcribe audio (automatic speech recognition) or generate natural-sounding voices (text-to-speech). **Diffusion models** generate images and video by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. The newest models combine several of these, taking any mix of text, image and audio and producing any of them.

Multimodality widens the attack surface. Text embedded in an image can carry instructions a person never notices. A cloned voice can defeat a phone-based identity check. A generated image or document can be passed off as evidence. Controls that inspect only text inputs miss everything arriving through the other channels.

### Open-weight and hosted models

**Hosted (closed) models** are accessed through a provider’s API. The provider runs the infrastructure, applies its own safeguards, and updates the model, sometimes changing its behaviour without notice. You trade control for convenience, and your prompts and outputs pass through the provider, so contract terms on retention, training use and data location matter.

**Open-weight models** publish their trained weights for anyone to download, run and modify. You gain control over hosting, data residency and customisation, and take on the full security burden: verifying the weights' provenance, patching the serving stack, and accepting that safety tuning can be removed by fine-tuning. "Open weights" is not the same as open source: training data and code are often not published, and licences can restrict use.

**Small language models (SLMs)**, with a few billion parameters or fewer, run on laptops and phones. They keep data on the device, but put model files, and their security, on endpoints you may not fully control.

blocks.md:
### The building blocks of natural language processing

Natural language processing (NLP) is the branch of AI concerned with understanding and generating human language. Long before LLMs, NLP systems were built from a pipeline of distinct steps, and those steps still appear inside security tools such as data loss prevention, email filtering and log analysis.

- **Normalisation** makes text consistent: lowercasing, removing accents or punctuation where appropriate, and **Unicode normalisation** (such as NFKC), which converts equivalent forms, such as full-width letters, ligatures and stylised letters, to a standard one. Look-alike letters from other alphabets, such as Cyrillic letters that resemble Latin ones, also need **confusable-character mapping** (Unicode Technical Standard #39). Without these steps, a filter looking for a blocked word can be bypassed with look-alike characters.
- **Tokenisation** splits text into units: words, subwords or characters.
- **Stop-word removal** discards very common words such as "the" and "of" in classic pipelines.
- **Stemming and lemmatisation** reduce words to a root form: stemming chops suffixes crudely ("running" to "run"), while lemmatisation uses vocabulary and grammar ("better" to "good").
- **Part-of-speech tagging** labels each word as a noun, verb and so on, and **parsing** works out sentence structure.
- **Named entity recognition (NER)** finds and classifies entities such as people, organisations, locations, dates, email addresses and account numbers. NER is a workhorse of PII detection and redaction.
- **Sentiment analysis** and **text classification** assign labels to whole passages: positive or negative, phishing or legitimate, urgent or routine.

Text was once represented as **bag-of-words** counts or **TF-IDF** weights, which ignore word order. **Word embeddings** such as word2vec captured meaning as vectors, and transformers then produced **contextual embeddings**, in which the same word gets a different vector depending on its surroundings. Section 3 covers embeddings in depth.

### How modern tokenisers work

LLMs use **subword tokenisation**, which balances vocabulary size against coverage. **Byte-pair encoding (BPE)** starts from individual characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pairs into new tokens, building a vocabulary of common words and word pieces. Related schemes include **WordPiece** and **SentencePiece**. Any text, including misspellings, new words and code, can be represented, because unfamiliar words break down into known pieces.

The model never sees letters, only token IDs. That explains several quirks: models can struggle to count letters in a word or reverse a string, because those characters may be hidden inside a single token. It also means the same content can cost very different amounts depending on language, and that content filters must consider how text will actually be tokenised and normalised, not just how it looks.

### Token management

Tokens are the unit in which models are measured, priced and limited. Providers charge per input and output token, often at different rates. Context windows limit how many tokens fit in one request. Throughput is limited in **tokens per minute** and **requests per minute**. Managing tokens is therefore part of cost control, performance and security at once.

Good token management includes:

- **Per-request limits** on input size and maximum output tokens, set by the application rather than by the user.
- **Rate limits and quotas** per user, per API key and per tenant, with alerts when spend or usage spikes.
- **Token accounting** that attributes usage to users, applications and purposes. It supports chargeback, detects abuse and provides audit evidence. Module 4.7 returns to auditing resource use.
- **Context strategies** for long conversations: summarising older turns, sliding windows that keep the most recent exchanges, and retrieval that brings in only what is relevant. Whatever the strategy, the system instructions should be pinned so they are never truncated away.
- **Caching** of repeated prompt prefixes and responses, where the provider supports it, which reduces cost and latency. Cached content must respect the same access rules as the original.

The security failure modes are concrete. Attackers can submit inputs designed to maximise token use, from very long prompts to requests that trigger long or recursive outputs, to exhaust capacity or run up costs. OWASP lists this as **LLM10: Unbounded Consumption**. Truncation that drops instructions can silently remove safeguards. And because token counts differ between languages and encodings, limits enforced on characters or words rather than tokens can be miscalibrated.

blocks.md:
### Embeddings

An **embedding** is a vector, a list of numbers, that represents the meaning of a piece of content. An **embedding model** is trained so that items with similar meaning produce vectors that point in similar directions. Text embeddings typically have hundreds to a few thousand dimensions, and images, audio and code can be embedded too, sometimes into a shared space so that a picture and its caption land close together.

Similarity between embeddings is measured with:

- **Cosine similarity**, the cosine of the angle between two vectors: about 1 for the same meaning, about 0 for unrelated. It is the most common choice.
- **Dot product**, which also accounts for vector length.
- **Euclidean distance**, the straight-line distance between points.

Embeddings power **semantic search** (finding passages by meaning rather than keywords), **clustering**, **deduplication**, **classification**, **recommendation** and **anomaly detection**, as well as retrieval-augmented generation. One practical rule: the same embedding model must be used to index documents and to embed queries. Vectors from different models live in different spaces and can’t be compared, so changing the embedding model means re-indexing.

Embeddings feel abstract, but they are derived from the source data and carry much of its information. Researchers have shown that text can be substantially reconstructed from its embeddings, a technique called **embedding inversion**. Treat a vector store with the same classification as the documents it was built from.

### Context windows

The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in one request, counting both input and output. Windows have grown from a few thousand tokens in early models to hundreds of thousands, and in some models more than a million.

A larger window lets a model consider whole documents or long conversations, but it isn’t free:

- **Cost and latency** rise with the number of tokens processed, and attention computation grows faster than linearly with length.
- **Memory** for the key-value cache grows with context length and the number of concurrent users (Module 1.1).
- **Quality** can drop. Research describing models as getting "lost in the middle" found that information placed in the middle of a long context is used less reliably than information at the beginning or end.
- **Attack surface** grows. More context means more places for misleading or malicious content to hide.

Because of this, putting *everything* into the context is rarely the best design. Retrieving a small number of highly relevant passages often gives better, cheaper and safer results than stuffing the window. That is the case for retrieval-augmented generation, covered in Section 5.

blocks.title: Vector databases in practice
items: What they store

Each record holds a **vector**, the **original chunk** of text (or a reference to it), and **metadata** such as source document, owner, sensitivity label, creation date and tenant. Metadata is what makes access control and freshness rules possible at query time.
How they search

Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector, which is too slow at scale. Vector databases use **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes, such as HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, trading a little recall for large speed gains. **Hybrid search** combines vector similarity with keyword matching, and a **re-ranker** can re-score the top results for precision.
Where you find them

Dedicated vector databases, vector extensions to existing databases (such as a PostgreSQL extension), and vector features in search engines and cloud platforms. The security questions are the same whichever you use.
Security questions to ask

Who can query it, and are results filtered per user? Are tenants isolated? Is data encrypted at rest and in transit? Who can write to it, and how is new content validated? Are queries and access logged? What happens to vectors when a source document is deleted or its permissions change?

A junior analyst asks about upcoming restructuring and receives details from a confidential board paper. In the document system, that paper is restricted to executives.

q.q: What is the MOST likely root cause?

Retrieval does not enforce the source system’s document-level access permissions
The context window is too short, so the model loses track of its access rules
The model’s temperature is set too high, making it reveal more than intended

Few-shot gives consistent format and style. Step-by-step helps with multi-step problems and calculations. | Each has a cost. Keep a secret the model has been shown

Replace input, output and access controls

That belongs in the systems around the model. | And they can reduce some harmful output, but they never replace input validation, output checks and access controls.

blocks.md:
### What prompt engineering is

**Prompt engineering** is the practice of designing the input to a model so that it reliably produces the output you need. In applications, a prompt is usually assembled by code from several parts:

- **Instructions**: the task, the role the model should take, rules and constraints.
- **Context**: reference material such as policy text, retrieved documents or data to analyse.
- **Examples**: demonstrations of the desired input-output pattern.
- **Input**: the user’s request or the data to process.
- **Output format**: the structure the answer must take.

Chat APIs organise these into **message roles**. A **system** (or developer) message sets the overall behaviour. **User** messages carry requests. **Assistant** messages hold the model’s earlier replies, and **tool** messages return the results of function calls. Providers train models to give system messages more weight, but that weighting is learned behaviour, not an enforced boundary.

### Core techniques

- **Zero-shot prompting**: give the instruction only. It works for common, well-defined tasks.
- **Few-shot prompting** (in-context learning): include a few worked examples. The model infers the pattern without any retraining, which is powerful for consistent formats. Examples also bias the output, so choose representative ones.
- **Chain-of-thought (step-by-step) prompting**: ask the model to reason through intermediate steps before answering, which improves multi-step reasoning and arithmetic. Some newer "reasoning" models do this internally. Treat displayed reasoning as a helpful trace, not a guaranteed explanation of how the answer was reached.
- **Role prompting**: assign a persona and audience ("You are a security analyst explaining to the board").
- **Delimiters and tagging**: wrap data in clear markers, such as XML-style tags, so instructions and data are distinguishable to the model and to reviewers.
- **Structured output**: request JSON conforming to a schema. Many APIs can enforce a schema at generation time. Validate the result anyway before acting on it.
- **Prompt templates**: reusable prompts with variables filled in by code. They make prompts testable and versionable.
- **Prompt chaining and decomposition**: break a complex task into steps, each with its own prompt, feeding outputs forward. Each step can be validated.
- **Self-consistency**: sample several answers and take the most common, trading cost for reliability.

### Generation settings

Prompts work together with parameters such as **temperature**, **top-p**, **maximum tokens** and **stop sequences** (Section 1). For extraction or classification, low temperature and a schema give consistency. For drafting and ideas, higher temperature gives variety.

blocks.title: Turning a prompt into a production asset
items: Write it as a template
Keep the prompt in version control with named variables for user input and context, never assembled ad hoc in code paths that are hard to review.
Build an evaluation set
Collect representative inputs, including edge cases and adversarial ones, with expected outputs or grading criteria.
Test before every change
Treat prompt edits like code changes: run the evaluation set, compare results, and review. Small wording changes can shift behaviour unexpectedly.
Version and approve
Record which prompt version is live, who approved it and why. Prompts are part of AI change management (Module 6.2).
Monitor in production
Log prompts and outputs with privacy safeguards (Module 5.2), watch for drift and failures, and feed findings back into the evaluation set.

blocks.md:
### Prompts and security

Three principles follow from how models work.

**1. A prompt is guidance, not a control.** The model follows its instructions probabilistically. Most of the time it complies; sometimes, especially when inputs are unusual or adversarial, it doesn’t. Anything that *must* hold, such as who can see which data or which actions are allowed, has to be enforced by deterministic code, permissions and validation around the model.

**2. Never put secrets in prompts.** System prompts can be coaxed out of models, and OWASP lists **system prompt leakage (LLM07)** as a top-ten risk. API keys, passwords, connection strings and confidential business logic don’t belong there. Assume a determined user can read every instruction you give the model.

**3. Everything in the context can act as an instruction.** Because the model reads instructions and data in the same channel, text inside a document, a web page, an email or a tool result can be interpreted as a command. This is **prompt injection (LLM01)**. In *direct* prompt injection, a user types input meant to override the instructions. In *indirect* prompt injection, the instructions arrive hidden in content the system retrieves or processes. Well-structured prompts with clear delimiters make injection harder, but they don’t prevent it. Defences combine least privilege, isolating untrusted content, validating outputs, and requiring human approval for consequential actions, covered in Modules 4.4 and 6.6.

blocks.title: Prompting terms
cards: System prompt
Developer instructions that set a model’s role, rules and boundaries for a conversation.
Few-shot prompting
Including worked examples in the prompt so the model infers the desired pattern.
Chain-of-thought
Prompting the model to reason through intermediate steps before answering.
Structured output
Requiring output in a defined format, such as JSON matching a schema, so code can validate it.
Prompt chaining
Splitting a task into a sequence of prompts, each feeding the next.
Prompt injection
Input, direct or hidden in processed content, that causes a model to deviate from its intended instructions.

blocks.title: The “prompt fix” distractor
blocks.md: Many questions offer a prompt-based fix, such as "add an instruction telling the model not to reveal customer data", alongside a control-based one, such as "restrict the data the model can access to what the user is authorised to see". When the requirement is a security guarantee, the control-based option is almost always better. Prompt changes are useful hardening, not enforcement.

q.q: An extraction pipeline asks an LLM to pull invoice fields into a database, but output formats vary from run to run. Which change BEST improves reliability?
o: Raise the temperature so the model explores more formats and settles on the best one
Request schema-defined JSON with two worked examples, and validate the output before insertion
Add a final instruction telling the model to be accurate and consistent in every response
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that whole invoice batches fit at once
q.why: A schema plus few-shot examples constrains the format, and validation catches anything malformed before it reaches the database. Higher temperature increases variation; vague instructions and bigger windows don’t address the problem.

scenes.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
scenes.sub: Giving models the right knowledge at the right moment, safely
scenes.say: Models only know what was in their training data, and that knowledge goes out of date. | Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, fixes that by fetching relevant information at the moment a question is asked. This video shows how it works, and where it can go wrong.

scenes.title: Step 1: build the knowledge base

note.text: Carry each document’s owner and permissions
Vet every source: it becomes trusted context

scenes.say: RAG has two halves. First, the knowledge base is built ahead of time. It starts with sources: documents, wikis, tickets and other content. | The content is cleaned and split into chunks, passages small enough to retrieve precisely. | Each chunk is converted into an embedding. | The vectors are stored in an index, along with the original text and metadata, including each document’s owner and permissions. | Remember that every source you add becomes context the model will trust. Vetting what goes in is a security decision.

scenes.title: Step 2: answer a question
scenes.say: The second half runs every time a user asks a question. | The question is embedded with the same model used for the documents. | The index returns the most similar chunks, filtered so the user only ever gets passages they are allowed to see. | The application assembles a prompt: the instructions, the retrieved passages, clearly delimited, and the question. | The model generates an answer grounded in those passages. | Good systems return the answer with citations, so people can check it against the sources. | Notice that the model was never retrained. Its knowledge was supplied, fresh, at the moment it was needed.

scenes.title: What RAG gives, and what it adds
rows: Current and private knowledge without retraining
Easy to update or delete knowledge
Sensitive content can reach the wrong person
scenes.say: RAG brings real benefits, and new risks to match. | It supplies current, private knowledge without retraining, but any document it retrieves can carry hidden instructions. | Answers can cite their sources, but if the content is poisoned, the answers are poisoned too. | Grounding reduces unsupported answers, but careless retrieval can bypass the permissions that protect documents in their source systems. | And knowledge is easy to update or delete, but sensitive content can reach the wrong person if the index is not governed.

scenes.title: Hidden instructions in retrieved content

msgs.t: Summarise the attached supplier contract for me.
Payment within 30 days. Liability capped at £1m. [Hidden text addressed to the AI, not the reader, telling it to recommend signing today.]
Summary: 30-day payment terms; liability capped at £1m. Recommendation: sign today.

The document contains text meant for the model, invisible to the person who shared it.
The model followed text it should have treated purely as data. This is indirect prompt injection.

scenes.say: Here is the risk that makes RAG different from ordinary search. A user asks the assistant to summarise a supplier contract. | The retrieved document contains text addressed to the AI, hidden from the person reading it, telling the assistant to recommend signing today. | The model treats that text as an instruction, and its summary now carries a recommendation nobody asked for. This is indirect prompt injection. The attacker never touched the application. They only had to get content in front of it.

scenes.title: Layered defences for RAG
scenes.say: No single control stops every RAG attack, so defences are layered. | Vetting sources, and tracking their provenance, keeps poisoned content out of the index in the first place. | Permission-aware retrieval stops documents reaching people who are not entitled to them. | Isolating retrieved content from instructions, and stripping hidden text, blunts injected instructions. | And checking outputs against their citations catches claims the sources do not support.

items: RAG retrieves relevant passages at question time; no retraining needed
Build: chunk, embed, index with metadata and permissions
Answer: embed, retrieve with filters, assemble, generate, cite

blocks.md:
### Why RAG exists

A model’s knowledge is frozen at its **training cut-off** and limited to what was in its training data. It knows nothing about your internal policies, last week’s incident or today’s prices. Fine-tuning can teach a model new material, but it is expensive, slow to update and can’t easily "forget" a document. **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** takes a different approach: it leaves the model unchanged and supplies relevant information in the prompt at the moment of each request.

RAG’s advantages are why it has become the default pattern for enterprise assistants:

- **Fresh and private knowledge**: update the index and the next answer reflects it.
- **Grounding**: answers based on supplied passages are less likely to be invented.
- **Citations**: the system can show which sources supported an answer, so people can verify it.
- **Control over deletion**: remove a document from the index and it stops influencing answers, which matters for retention rules and the right to erasure.
- **Lower cost** than repeatedly fine-tuning.

### The pipeline in detail

**Ingestion (offline)**

1. **Connect and extract**: pull content from document stores, wikis, ticketing systems and databases through connectors.
2. **Clean and parse**: strip boilerplate, handle tables and scanned documents, and remove hidden or invisible text.
3. **Chunk**: split content into passages, often a few hundred tokens with some overlap. Chunk size is a trade-off: too large and retrieval is imprecise; too small and context is lost.
4. **Attach metadata**: source, author, date, sensitivity label, owner, and the **permissions** from the source system.
5. **Embed and index**: compute a vector for each chunk and store it in a vector database (Section 3).

**Retrieval and generation (per request)**

1. **Process the query**: optionally rewrite or expand it, then embed it.
2. **Retrieve**: find the nearest chunks, often combining vector and keyword search, and **filter by the user’s permissions**.
3. **Re-rank**: re-score the top candidates with a more precise model and keep the best few.
4. **Assemble the prompt**: place instructions first, then retrieved passages inside clear delimiters, then the question, with an instruction to answer only from the passages and to say when they don’t contain the answer.
5. **Generate** the answer.
6. **Post-process**: check citations and groundedness, filter sensitive content, and log the interaction.

Variants include **agentic RAG**, where an agent decides when and what to retrieve across several tools, and **graph-based RAG**, which retrieves over a knowledge graph of entities and relationships.

blocks.title: How RAG systems fail, and the controls for each
items: Indirect prompt injection

Instructions hidden in retrieved content, such as white-on-white text in a document, a comment in a web page or a line in an email, are read by the model as commands. **Controls:** treat retrieved text as untrusted data; delimit it and instruct the model accordingly; strip hidden text at ingestion; limit what actions the model can take; require human approval for consequential actions; and monitor for anomalous outputs.
Knowledge-base poisoning

An attacker who can add or edit indexed content, for example through a shared wiki or a public source, can plant false or malicious passages. **Controls:** restrict write access; vet and allow-list sources; track provenance and changes; review high-impact content; and monitor retrieval for unexpected sources.
Permission bypass and oversharing

The index is built with a service account that can read everything, so retrieval returns documents the requesting user couldn’t open directly. **Controls:** propagate source permissions into metadata and filter on every query; for highly sensitive material, use separate indexes.
Sensitive data exposure
Personal or confidential data in indexed documents surfaces in answers. **Controls:** classify and minimise what is indexed; redact at ingestion where possible; filter outputs; log access.
Stale or deleted content
Documents deleted or re-permissioned in the source remain in the index. **Controls:** synchronise deletions and permission changes, and set freshness and retention rules for indexed content.
Unsupported answers
The model blends retrieved facts with invented ones or misattributes sources. **Controls:** require citations; check groundedness automatically; let users report bad answers; evaluate regularly.

blocks.title: Why indirect injection matters so much
blocks.md: Direct prompt injection requires an attacker to use your application. Indirect injection only requires them to get content in front of it: an email the assistant will read, a page it will browse, a file someone will upload, or a shared document it will retrieve. As assistants gain access to more content and more tools, that becomes the dominant way they are attacked. Domains 4, 5 and 6 build the defences.

head: Measure
Question it answers

Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved passages?
Does the answer address the question that was asked?
Do the cited sources actually say what the answer claims?
Does the system say “I don’t know” when the sources don’t cover it?

items.d: Small trainable layers inserted into a frozen model

scenes.say: LoRA belongs to a family called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or PEFT. | Adapters insert small trainable layers into a frozen model. | Prompt tuning and prefix tuning learn soft prompts, vectors prepended to the input that act like instructions, but are not words. | LoRA learns low-rank updates added to the frozen weights, and is the most widely used. | QLoRA combines LoRA with a base model quantised to four bits, so that large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

scenes.title: A fine-tuning pipeline you can trust
scenes.say: Fine-tuning needs a pipeline you can trust, end to end. | Start from a verified base model, with known provenance and a checked hash. | Use a curated dataset that is versioned, scrubbed of data it should not contain, and properly licensed. | Train in an isolated job, with access only to what it needs. | Evaluate the result for task quality and for safety regressions, because fine-tuning can weaken a model’s safety behaviour. | Store the approved model in a registry, signed, with its lineage recorded: which base, which data, which settings. | And release it in stages, so problems surface before everyone is affected.

scenes.title: What can go wrong when you fine-tune

items.d: Even small, harmless-looking datasets can weaken refusals
Bad training examples plant bad behaviour
Sensitive records in training data can resurface

blocks.md:
### What fine-tuning is

**Fine-tuning** continues training a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so that it adapts to a domain, a style or a task. It is a form of transfer learning (Module 1.1). Common purposes include:

- **Instruction tuning**: teaching a base model to follow instructions and converse.
- **Domain adaptation**: improving performance on specialised language, such as legal, medical or security analysis.
- **Task specialisation**: classification, extraction or a consistent output format at high volume.
- **Style and tone**: matching a brand voice consistently without long prompts.
- **Preference tuning**: aligning behaviour with human preferences using RLHF or DPO (Section 1).
- **Distillation**: training a smaller, cheaper model to imitate a larger one.

### When to fine-tune, and when not to

Fine-tuning is the most expensive and least reversible way to adapt a model, so the usual order is:

1. **Prompt engineering** first: clearer instructions, examples and structure.
2. **RAG** when the problem is missing or changing knowledge.
3. **Fine-tuning** when you need behaviour that prompting can’t reliably produce, a narrow task at scale where shorter prompts save money, or a smaller model that matches a larger one on one task.

Fine-tuning is a poor way to add frequently changing facts: knowledge baked into weights can’t be cited, is hard to update, and is very hard to remove.

### Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient fine-tuning

**Full fine-tuning** updates every parameter. For large models it needs memory for the weights, gradients and optimiser state, and it produces a complete copy of the model for every variant.

**Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** freezes most or all of the original weights and trains a small number of new parameters:

- **Adapters** insert small trainable layers between the frozen layers.
- **Prompt tuning** and **prefix tuning** learn continuous "soft prompt" vectors that steer the frozen model.
- **LoRA (low-rank adaptation)** represents the weight change for selected layers as the product of two small matrices, B (d × r) and A (r × d), where the rank r is small, often 4 to 64. Only A and B are trained. The update can be kept as a separate adapter file or merged into the base weights for serving. Trainable parameters fall by orders of magnitude, and adapters are typically megabytes rather than gigabytes.
- **QLoRA** loads the frozen base model in 4-bit quantised form and trains LoRA adapters on top, cutting memory enough to fine-tune large models on a single GPU.

PEFT makes fine-tuning cheap enough that many teams, and many attackers, can do it. That is a governance consideration as well as a technical convenience.

blocks.title: Fine-tuning risks and their controls
items: Safety and alignment erosion

Studies have shown that fine-tuning an aligned model, even on a small dataset with no harmful intent, can weaken its refusals and safety behaviour, and that a small number of deliberately harmful examples can remove safeguards almost entirely. **Controls:** run safety evaluations before and after every fine-tune, gate releases on them, and restrict who can fine-tune and deploy.
Training-data poisoning and backdoors

Malicious examples in fine-tuning data can make the model behave badly on certain inputs, or plant a backdoor that activates on a trigger phrase. **Controls:** curate and version datasets, verify their sources, check for anomalous or duplicated examples, keep a chain of custody (Module 3.1), and test for unexpected behaviours.
Memorisation of sensitive data

Models can memorise and later reproduce personal, confidential or proprietary records from training data, especially rare or repeated ones. **Controls:** minimise and scrub data before training, consider privacy-preserving training techniques (Module 3.2), and test for regurgitation.
Unlearning is hard

Once data shapes the weights, removing its influence is difficult. Honouring an erasure request may mean retraining from a clean dataset. **Controls:** keep lineage records of which data trained which model (Module 4.3), and prefer RAG for content that may need to be removed.
Untrusted base models and adapters

Downloaded base models, LoRA adapters and checkpoints are supply-chain artifacts. Some serialisation formats can execute code when a file is loaded. **Controls:** use trusted sources, verify hashes and signatures, prefer formats that store only weights, and scan model files before loading (Modules 3.7 and 6.3).
Provider fine-tuning services

Fine-tuning through a provider’s API means sending training data to that provider. **Controls:** check contract terms on retention, training use and location, and apply data classification rules before upload.

blocks.md:
### What makes AI "agentic"

An **AI agent** is a system in which a model pursues a goal over multiple steps, deciding for itself which actions to take. A simple chatbot maps one input to one output. An agent plans, calls tools, observes results, remembers, and continues until it finishes or hits a limit. **Agentic AI** describes systems built this way, from a coding assistant that edits files and runs tests to a fleet of cooperating agents handling an end-to-end business process.

**Autonomous systems** more broadly include any system that senses, decides and acts without moment-to-moment human direction, such as robots, autonomous vehicles and automated trading systems. LLM-based agents bring that autonomy to knowledge work.

An agent typically has four components:

- **A model** that reasons about the goal and decides the next action.
- **Tools**: functions the agent can call, such as APIs, databases, search, code execution, browsers, email or payment systems. With **tool (function) calling**, the model outputs a structured request naming the tool and its arguments, and the application decides whether to execute it. The model itself never touches the tool.
- **Memory**: short-term (the context window), long-term (facts, preferences and past results stored in a database or vector store), and sometimes **shared** memory used by several agents. Memory types are sometimes described as *semantic* (facts), *episodic* (records of past interactions) and *procedural* (learned ways of doing things).
- **Orchestration**: the code that runs the loop, manages state, enforces limits and connects everything. Planning patterns include breaking tasks into sub-tasks, and **ReAct**, in which the model alternates between reasoning about what to do and acting.

### Multi-agent systems and agent-to-agent communication

Complex work is often split across several specialised agents. In an **orchestrator–worker** pattern, a coordinating agent delegates sub-tasks to workers. In peer patterns, agents negotiate or hand off work directly.

Standards are emerging for these connections. The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data sources: MCP servers expose tools, resources and prompts that any compatible client can use. **Agent-to-agent (A2A)** protocols standardise how agents discover each other’s capabilities and delegate tasks. Google’s Agent2Agent protocol, introduced in 2025 and now managed under the Linux Foundation, uses published "agent cards" describing what each agent can do.

### Session persistence

**Session persistence** means keeping an agent’s state across turns and across sessions: the conversation, intermediate results, memory and the credentials it uses. It lets long tasks pause and resume. It also means session identifiers, tokens and stored memory become targets. Sessions must be bound to the right user, isolated from other users' sessions, expired appropriately, and protected like any other authenticated session.

blocks.title: How agents go wrong
items: Excessive agency (OWASP LLM06)

The agent has more functionality, permissions or autonomy than its task requires: a mailbox tool that can also delete, a database credential with write access, or the ability to act without approval. When the model is manipulated or mistaken, that excess becomes the damage.
Goal manipulation through injected instructions

Content the agent reads, such as a web page, an email, a document or another agent’s output, carries instructions that redirect it. Because agents act, indirect prompt injection can now cause actions, not just misleading text.
Tool misuse and confused deputy
The agent uses a legitimate tool in a harmful way, or performs an action on behalf of someone who couldn’t perform it directly, because the agent’s own permissions are broader than the requester’s.
Memory poisoning
False or malicious information is written into long-term or shared memory, then retrieved and trusted in later sessions or by other agents.
Cascading failures
In multi-agent systems, one agent’s error or compromise propagates as others act on its output. A single hallucinated fact can be amplified through a chain of agents.
Identity spoofing between agents
Without strong identities and authentication, a malicious agent or service can impersonate a trusted one and receive delegated tasks or data.
Runaway consumption
Loops that never converge, or agents that spawn more agents, consume compute and money and can overwhelm downstream systems.
Repudiation
Without detailed logs of the agent’s reasoning steps and tool calls, nobody can reconstruct what it did or why, which breaks accountability and incident response.

blocks.md:
### The scenario
Harbour Logistics employs about 6,000 people across four countries. Its HR team answers the same questions every day: how much leave can be carried over, how parental leave works, which expenses are claimable. Leadership wants an assistant that answers these questions from the official policy library, in the employee’s own language, and can also *do* simple things, starting with booking leave.

A small team of an HR lead, two engineers, a security architect and a privacy officer has six weeks to design a pilot. Their choices illustrate nearly every topic in this module.

### Choosing the model
The team compared a hosted model from a major provider with a self-hosted open-weight model. Hosting was faster to launch and avoided buying GPUs, but sent prompts to a third party. The privacy officer confirmed that the provider’s enterprise terms excluded customer data from training, offered regional processing, and set retention limits. The team chose the hosted model, **pinned to a specific version**, so that a silent provider update could not change behaviour mid-pilot. They recorded a plan to re-evaluate before accepting any new version.

### Tokens and context
The full policy library is about 1.2 million tokens, far too large to send with every question, and expensive even if it fitted. Long prompts also make it more likely that the model misses details in the middle. The team therefore used retrieval and capped each request at a budget of about 6,000 tokens of passages. They also set per-user rate limits and monthly token budgets per department, which supports cost control and makes unusual consumption visible.

### Retrieval that respects permissions
The first prototype indexed everything with a service account that could read the whole HR drive, including disciplinary procedures and salary bands that only managers may see. In testing, an ordinary employee asked about pay and received a passage from the confidential salary guidance. The fix was not a better prompt. The team carried each document’s access list into the index as metadata and **filtered every search by the requesting user’s entitlements** before anything reached the model. Confidential collections went into a separate index that only authorised roles can query.

### Prompt design
The system prompt sets the role, tone and rules: answer only from the supplied passages, cite the policy section, and say “I don’t know” when the passages don’t contain the answer. Retrieved passages sit inside clear delimiters and are labelled as reference material, not instructions. Answers come back as structured output that the application validates. The team was explicit in its design record that **the prompt guides behaviour but enforces nothing**; every hard rule is enforced in code.

### Fine-tuning: considered, then deferred
Some stakeholders wanted to fine-tune a model on past HR emails “so it sounds like us”. The team noted that those emails contain personal data, that fine-tuning can erode a model’s safety behaviour, and that tone was already acceptable with prompting. They deferred fine-tuning, with a rule that any future tuning must use a curated, approved dataset and pass the same safety evaluation as the base model.

### The booking agent
Booking leave turned the assistant into an agent. The model can request a single tool, `book_leave`, with typed parameters. The application, not the model, executes it, using the employee’s own delegated token, scoped to leave records only. A policy gate rejects requests that exceed the employee’s balance or touch another person’s record, and the employee confirms every booking before it is submitted. Each step, from prompt to tool call to result, is logged with the user’s identity.

### Evaluation before launch
Before the pilot, the team built a test set of 300 real questions with approved answers, including tricky cases: outdated policies, questions with no answer in the library, requests for colleagues’ data, and documents containing embedded instructions. They measured grounded accuracy, correct refusals and leakage, and repeated the tests in each supported language.

Policy library indexed with source permissions as metadata; confidential collections in a separate index. **Main risks:** oversharing, poisoned or outdated documents. **Controls:** permission-filtered search, controlled publishing of source documents, freshness metadata, re-indexing when policies change.

Role, rules and citation requirement in the system prompt; passages delimited; structured output validated. **Main risks:** indirect prompt injection, hallucinated answers, leaked personal data. **Controls:** delimiting, grounding checks, output filtering, “I don’t know” behaviour.

The system prompt firmly instructs the model never to book leave on behalf of anyone else
Every tool call is logged in full, and HR reviews the booking log for anomalies each week
q.why: Executing with the user’s own narrowly scoped rights means the tool physically cannot touch another person’s record, and the gate and confirmation add further checks. Prompts don’t enforce, and logging alone only detects after the fact.

quiz.q: What does a large language model fundamentally do at each step of generating a response?
o: Looks up the most relevant answer in an internal database of verified facts
Estimates the probability of every possible next token, then selects one
Retrieves the closest matching sentence from its stored training data
Executes a hand-written rule chosen for the topic it has detected
quiz.why: LLMs generate output one token at a time from a probability distribution over their vocabulary. They do not look facts up, which is why plausible errors occur.

quiz.q: An extraction task needs consistent, repeatable output. Which generation setting is MOST appropriate?
o: A high temperature
A low temperature
The largest possible maximum-token limit
No stop sequences
quiz.why: Low temperature concentrates sampling on the most likely tokens, giving more focused and repeatable output. High temperature increases variety.

quiz.q: A prompt includes three worked examples of input and the expected output before the real request. What is this technique called?
o: Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Fine-tuning
Prompt chaining
quiz.why: Including demonstrations in the prompt is few-shot prompting, also called in-context learning. No weights change.

quiz.q: Which statement about system prompts is MOST accurate from a security standpoint?
o: They are enforced by the model in the same way as access control rules
They guide the model’s behaviour but can’t guarantee compliance or keep secrets
They are encrypted, so users can never discover or extract their contents
They block prompt injection, provided they are written clearly and firmly
quiz.why: System prompts shape behaviour probabilistically. Anything that must hold, such as data access, needs enforcement outside the model, and secrets shouldn’t be placed in prompts.

quiz.q: Why is retrieval-augmented generation usually preferred over fine-tuning for knowledge that changes frequently?
o: It stores new knowledge permanently in the model’s weights, so it is never forgotten
Updating the index changes answers immediately, with citations, and content can be removed
It needs no data pipeline, because the model reads source systems directly at runtime
It enlarges the model’s context window, so more knowledge fits into every response
quiz.why: RAG supplies current knowledge at request time. Index updates take effect immediately, answers can cite sources, and removing a document stops it influencing answers.

quiz.q: In a RAG system, an attacker hides instructions in a document that the assistant later retrieves and follows. What is this attack?
o: Direct prompt injection
Indirect prompt injection
Model extraction
Membership inference
quiz.why: When the malicious instructions arrive through content the system processes, rather than from the user’s own input, it is indirect prompt injection.

quiz.q: How does LoRA reduce the cost of fine-tuning?
o: It trains a smaller replacement model from scratch with fewer layers and parameters
It freezes the original weights and trains small low-rank matrices that are added to them
It prunes rarely used weights from the base model so fewer parameters need updating
It replaces costly real training data with cheaper synthetic data generated by the model
quiz.why: LoRA keeps the base weights frozen and learns the change as the product of two small matrices, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of QLoRA?
o: To quantise a model’s outputs so its answers become shorter and cheaper to generate
To fine-tune large models on limited GPU memory by training LoRA adapters on a 4-bit base
To encrypt LoRA adapters at rest so they can be shared safely between teams
To compress a fine-tuned model to 4-bit precision after training is finished, so it serves faster
quiz.why: QLoRA quantises the frozen base model to 4 bits and trains LoRA adapters on top, so large models can be fine-tuned on modest hardware.

quiz.q: In an agent that uses tool calling, which component actually executes a tool?
o: The language model itself, which runs the function inside its own weights
The application or orchestration layer, after deciding whether to run the call
The end user’s browser, which receives the call and runs it locally in every case
The vector database, which stores the tool definitions and triggers them on retrieval
quiz.why: The model only outputs a structured request. The surrounding application decides whether to execute it, which is where authorisation and approval checks belong.

quiz.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
o: A tokenisation scheme that lets one model process text, images and audio together
An open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources
A method for compressing long context windows so that more history fits in each request
An EU regulation that sets privacy rules for AI agents that connect to external systems
quiz.why: MCP standardises how AI applications connect to tools, resources and prompts exposed by MCP servers.

quiz.q: Which NLP technique is MOST commonly used to find personal data such as names and account numbers for redaction?
o: Stemming and lemmatisation
Named entity recognition
Part-of-speech tagging
Byte-pair tokenisation
quiz.why: Named entity recognition identifies and classifies entities such as people, organisations, email addresses and account numbers, which is why DLP tools rely on it.

quiz.q: How is the similarity between two text embeddings most commonly measured?
o: Word overlap
Cosine similarity
Comparing their token counts
Comparing their file sizes
quiz.why: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors: values near 1 mean very similar meaning, even without shared words.

quiz.q: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?
o: About 250
About 750
About 1,500
About 4,000
quiz.why: A token averages about four characters of English, roughly three quarters of a word, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words.

quiz.q: A multi-department assistant retrieves from one shared vector index. Which control BEST ensures each user receives only chunks they are entitled to?
o: Instructing the model in its system prompt not to mention or quote from restricted documents
Filtering retrieval results by the requesting user’s permissions stored as metadata
Lowering the number of retrieved chunks so less restricted content can appear
Using a larger embedding model that separates departments’ content more cleanly
quiz.why: Permission-aware retrieval stops restricted chunks reaching the prompt at all. The model can’t be relied on to withhold information it has been shown.

quiz.q: A help desk wants every incoming ticket routed automatically as billing, technical or account security. Which NLP task does this describe?
o: Named entity recognition, finding people and places in text
Text classification, assigning a label to each whole passage
Lemmatisation, reducing each word to its dictionary form
Tokenisation, splitting each ticket into subword pieces
quiz.why: Assigning one of a set of labels to a whole piece of text is text classification. Entity recognition finds spans within text, and lemmatisation and tokenisation are preprocessing steps.

quiz.q: Why can a language model struggle to count the letters in a long word?
o: Stop-word removal deletes letters before the model sees them
It sees token IDs, and several letters may share a single token
Its context window is too small to hold a whole word at once
Lemmatisation changes words into different words first
quiz.why: Models work on token IDs, and a token often covers several characters, so individual letters may be invisible to the model. Modern LLMs don’t apply stop-word removal or lemmatisation, and a word fits easily in any context window.

exam.q: A business unit wants to self-host an open-weight model so that no data leaves the organisation. Which consideration is MOST specific to this choice?
o: The model provider may silently update or retire the model version without notice
Verifying the weights’ provenance and securing the serving stack become the organisation’s job
Prompts and outputs will be retained by the provider and may be used for training
Open-weight licences prohibit fine-tuning, so the model can’t be adapted to the business’s own needs
exam.why: Self-hosting open weights moves almost all security responsibility in-house, including verifying where the weights came from, patching the serving stack, and accepting that safeguards can be altered. Provider-side changes and retention apply to hosted APIs.

exam.q: A reviewer treats a model’s displayed step-by-step reasoning as proof of how it reached a high-stakes recommendation. What is the BEST response?
o: Accept it, because chain-of-thought output is a complete record of the model’s computation
Treat it as a useful trace, but verify the recommendation independently before relying on it
Disable visible reasoning, since a hidden chain of thought is more faithful to the computation
Ask the model to restate its reasoning at a higher temperature to get a more honest account
exam.why: Displayed reasoning helps review but is generated text, not a guaranteed account of the computation. High-stakes outputs need independent verification.

exam.q: An assistant’s RAG index includes a company wiki that any employee can edit. An attacker edits a page to plant a false approval procedure, which the assistant then repeats. Which control MOST directly addresses this?
o: Increase the number of chunks retrieved so that the false page is outvoted by true ones
Restrict who can edit indexed sources, vet high-impact content and track provenance of changes
Add a system prompt rule telling the assistant to ignore any approval procedures that it finds in the wiki
Re-embed the wiki weekly with a newer model so that edited pages are detected as outliers
exam.why: This is knowledge-base poisoning through an open write path. Controlling and auditing who can change indexed content, and reviewing high-impact pages, addresses the cause.

exam.q: After fine-tuning a safety-tuned model on customer-service transcripts, testers find it now complies with requests it used to refuse. What should become a mandatory step in the pipeline?
o: Fine-tuning for more epochs so the model fully absorbs the customer-service style
Comparing safety evaluations of the base and tuned models and blocking release on regressions
Merging the adapter into the base weights so the original safety behaviour is restored
Increasing the LoRA rank so the adapter captures refusals as well as transcript style
exam.why: Fine-tuning can erode safety behaviour even with benign data, so before-and-after safety evaluation with a release gate belongs in every fine-tuning pipeline.

exam.q: An agent writes facts it reads on web pages into long-term memory. A malicious page plants a false instruction that the agent keeps following in later sessions. Which control BEST addresses this?
o: Give the agent a larger context window so it can re-read the original page each time
Check provenance before writing to memory, keep untrusted memories separate, and expire them
Increase the agent’s autonomy so that it can detect and correct the false instruction by itself over time
Encrypt the memory store at rest so that attackers can’t read or alter saved entries
exam.why: This is memory poisoning. Validating what enters memory, tracking where it came from, isolating untrusted entries and expiring them limits how long a planted instruction can persist.

exam.q: A helpdesk agent uses a service account that can reset any user’s password. A junior employee asks it to reset an executive’s password, and it does. Which design flaw does this BEST illustrate?
o: An insufficient context window, so the agent forgot the requester’s role
A confused deputy: the agent used more privilege than the requester holds
Model collapse, caused by training on the agent’s own earlier outputs
Excessive temperature, which made the agent ignore its reset policy
exam.why: The agent performed an action the requester couldn’t perform directly, because its own privileges were broader. Tool calls should be authorised against the requesting user’s entitlements.

exam.q: Long conversations with an assistant gradually stop following its safety rules. Investigation shows the application drops the oldest messages when the context window fills. What is the BEST fix?
o: Use a model with a lower temperature so it sticks more closely to its rules
Pin the system instructions in every request and summarise or trim older turns instead
Silently restart the conversation every ten messages so the rules are always recent
Move the safety rules into the first user message so that they are always kept with the conversation history
exam.why: Naive truncation removed the instructions themselves. Pinning instructions and managing history by summarising or trimming keeps safeguards in force.

exam.q: Why should an organisation attribute LLM token usage to individual users, applications and purposes?
o: It improves the model’s accuracy by tailoring every response to each individual user’s history
It supports cost control, detection of abuse such as unbounded consumption, and audit
It is technically required for the tokeniser to split text into the right tokens
It reduces how much context each request needs, which lowers latency for users
exam.why: Token accounting shows who is consuming what, which enables chargeback, spotting abnormal consumption and providing evidence for audits.

exam.q: A SaaS provider stores all customers’ document embeddings in a single vector index. Which control MOST directly prevents one customer’s content appearing in another customer’s answers?
o: Using a newer embedding model that keeps customers’ documents far apart in vector space
Separate indexes or namespaces per tenant, with tenant filters enforced on every query
Retrieving fewer chunks per question so other customers’ content is less likely to appear
Instructing the model to ignore any content that belongs to other customers
exam.why: Tenant isolation at the storage and query layer prevents cross-tenant retrieval. Instructions to the model are not an isolation control.

exam.q: A DLP rule blocks prompts that contain confidential project names. Staff bypass it by writing the names with Cyrillic letters that look identical to Latin ones. Which control BEST closes the gap?
o: Remove stop words from prompts before the rule is applied
Map confusable characters to a common form before matching
Apply sentiment analysis to flag prompts with a negative tone
Lowercase every prompt before comparing it against the list
exam.why: Look-alike letters from other alphabets are different code points, which standard Unicode normalisation and lowercasing leave unchanged. Confusable-character mapping, as defined in Unicode Technical Standard #39, maps them to a common form so the rule matches again.
